# Atlassian Machine Learning Engineer Interview Process

[← Atlassian](README.md) · [Every Atlassian question](../atlassian.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/atlassian-machine-learning-engineer-interview-process)

---

The surprising rejection on this track has nothing to do with machine learning. One candidate designed a cross-product retrieval system over Jira and Confluence in the screen, handled the internal-chatbot design round well, came out of the behavioral round positive — and was rejected for not finishing the third extension of a moving-average coding problem inside a 60-minute session that also contained a second full problem. ML depth gets you through the screen and the design round; the generic data-structures session is what ends loops here, and it is graded on completeness under follow-up pressure rather than on approach. The pipeline also moves unusually fast — candidates report roughly two days between rounds — so there is no window to shore up the coding side once it starts.

## Interview Process

<!-- guide-diagram -->
![Atlassian Machine Learning Engineer interview process — the rounds in order](https://cgppcnnkwbfiieexbrea.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/guides/atlassian--machine-learning-engineer/process.webp)
<!-- guide-diagram -->

1. **Recruiter contact and screen (about 30 minutes).** Often inbound outreach rather than an application. The call covers your ML background, the products you would work near — retrieval and recommendation over issue tracker data, wiki pages and connected drives — target level, and logistics. Candidates on this track describe the recruiter scheduling fast, sometimes with next-round notification inside two days.

2. **ML phone screen with a senior machine learning engineer (about 60 minutes).** Three parts. A deep dive into one project from your resume: how the problem was framed, where the data came from, what you chose and why. Then fundamentals asked conversationally rather than as a quiz — bias-variance trade-offs, overfitting remedies, metric choice, imbalanced data — graded on reasoning about trade-offs, not definitions. Then a time-boxed design prompt; reported examples are a cross-product retrieval-augmented generation system spanning Jira and Confluence, a conventional recommendation template under time pressure, and a purely conversational chatbot design with no code at all.

3. **ML coding (onsite, virtual).** A hands-on session in a shared editor with no whiteboard, implementing an algorithm or data-pipeline component rather than answering theory. Requirements escalate mid-session, and the grading weighs clean, adaptable code — a structure you can extend when the definition changes — over the fastest first version.

4. **Algorithmic coding (onsite, typically 60 minutes, sometimes two problems in one session).** The hardest gate here. Reported problems: a streaming moving-average class over a fixed window with bounded memory, extended to a recency-weighted average and then a third variant; a tennis-court reservation system with availability checks and conflict detection; a doubly linked list with constant-time insert, delete and lookup; an ancestor query on a tree with a follow-up moving the structure to a directed acyclic graph; a digit-matching game with duplicate handling. The pattern is constant — a solvable core, then two or three mutations of the requirement in the same session.

5. **ML system design (onsite, typically 45 to 60 minutes).** The most track-specific round, and every reported prompt comes from a real internal problem: a chatbot answering employee questions from wiki pages and tickets; a search augmentation layer that classifies query intent as fact-seeking or task-seeking and surfaces a generated answer card above the normal results; a recommendation system for the issue tracker; a classifier that ingests bug reports from many client organizations and routes each to the right internal team. Interviewers push on the whole path — ingestion, chunking, embeddings, hybrid lexical-plus-vector retrieval, reranking, serving latency — then on evaluation, hallucination mitigation, retrieval versus fine-tuning, multi-tenant isolation, and the feedback loop for wrong predictions.

6. **Values and management (about 45 minutes for values, 60 for management, sometimes combined into one onsite block).** Scored separately from the technical rounds and tied to the five published values. Reported questions stay situational: a conflict with a teammate and how it resolved, pushing back on a decision, driving an improvement, helping a colleague grow, working through ambiguity, a mistake and the recovery, and why this company. The management portion adds role expectations and cross-functional collaboration.

7. **Decision.** Feedback between rounds can arrive within a couple of days while the pipeline is moving, but the end is where reports diverge: one candidate had sessions repeatedly cancelled and rescheduled, then heard nothing for a month after the onsite. Panels span Australia, New York and the Bay Area, so expect cross-time-zone video sessions throughout.

## What They Actually Evaluate

### ML System Design

One dedicated round of roughly 45 to 60 minutes, plus a compressed version inside the phone screen. Every reported prompt is retrieval or ranking over the company's own knowledge surfaces, so generic architecture answers underperform: the interviewer wants concrete sources, their access patterns, and what changes because the corpus is internal. Permission handling is the recurring hard requirement — candidates who skipped per-user access control at retrieval time were pushed on it immediately, because an assistant that surfaces a ticket the asker cannot see is a security defect, not a relevance miss. Signal also comes from evaluation: offline metrics, human review, hallucination detection, and catching a quality regression in production.

- [RAG Search Augmentation and Internal Chatbot](https://trueinterview.io/questions/rag-search-augmentation-internal-chatbot)
- [Role and Resource Access System](https://trueinterview.io/questions/role-and-resource-access-system)
- [Tagging System REST API](https://trueinterview.io/questions/tagging-system-rest-api)
- [Image Link Crawler Service](https://trueinterview.io/questions/image-link-crawler-service)

### Coding and Algorithm

One or two sessions at medium difficulty, and this is where the track's rejections concentrate. A session can carry two independent problems, which halves your time per problem and makes pacing part of the grade. Signal comes from naming the input and output contract before writing, keeping the structure modular enough that the second and third variants are edits rather than rewrites, and finishing with your own test walk. Signal is lost by pushing into the next extension while the previous one is unverified — the concrete failure mode is a candidate with a fully correct second problem and an unfinished third sub-part of the first, rejected on that alone.

- [Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree](../../questions/algorithm/lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree/README.md)
- [Smallest Department Covering Two Employees (LCA Variant on an Org Tree)](../../questions/object-oriented-programming/org-tree-lowest-common-department/README.md)
- [Expanding Tennis Club Court Assignment](https://trueinterview.io/questions/expanding-tennis-club-court-assignment)
- [Sequential, Deduped, and Parallel URL Fetcher](https://trueinterview.io/questions/sequential-deduped-parallel-url-fetcher)

### Low-Level Design

Much of the coding time is component design rather than puzzle solving: a stateful object with a fixed operation set, a complexity or memory target, and a definition that shifts under you. The reported instances are streaming structures — a window average that cannot store the full history, then a weighted variant with a running weighted sum; a linked structure with constant-time operations; counters that must return a maximum without scanning. State your invariant out loud, because the follow-ups are built to break it.

- [Commodity Price Checkpoints](https://trueinterview.io/questions/commodity-price-checkpoints)
- [Popular Content Counter](https://trueinterview.io/questions/popular-content-all-o-one)
- [Rate Limiter](../../questions/object-oriented-programming/rate-limiter/README.md)

### Behavioral and Leadership

A values conversation and a management conversation, both scored independently of the technical rounds. Interviewers on this track are described as friendly and willing to guide a stalled answer, which candidates sometimes misread as a low bar — the round still asks for a specific situation and then drills into your exact role and the outcome. The management portion adds role expectations and how you operate when requirements shift, which matters on teams where the target moves between quarters.

- [Atlassian Values and Management Rounds](guides/atlassian-values-and-management-rounds.md)

## What They Don't Test

- **Derivations and paper-level model trivia.** Fundamentals questions stay at the trade-off level — when a metric misleads, what to do about imbalance, why a model overfits. Rewarded instead is defending the choice you actually made on a real project.
- **Training-infrastructure heroics.** No reported round asks about distributed training, GPU scheduling or custom kernels. The design rounds care about ingestion, chunking, retrieval, ranking, serving latency and evaluation.
- **Modeling-competition technique.** Leaderboard tuning and feature-engineering tricks do not appear; multi-tenant isolation, permission-aware retrieval and feedback loops for wrong predictions do.
- **Whiteboard performance.** Onsite rounds are virtual and run in a shared editor, so practice typing working code with someone watching rather than sketching pseudocode.
- **Breadth over depth on your resume.** The screen picks one project and goes down into it; a wide list of models you have touched is worth less than one project you can defend from data collection through deployment.

## The Real Filter

The primary filter is the generic data-structures round, not the ML rounds. Candidates prepare retrieval architectures, evaluation strategy and their project narrative, then meet a coding session that packs two problems into an hour and grows each one twice. Because the ML content is the reason they are in the room, the coding session gets the least preparation and the least respect — and it produced the clearest documented rejection on this track, with strong design and behavioral feedback attached to the same loop. The fix is unglamorous: rehearse streaming-state problems until the second and third variants are mechanical, and protect the last minutes for verification rather than for one more extension.

The second pattern is designing a retrieval system as though the corpus were public. Every reported ML design conversation turned toward permissions, tenancy and privacy — which employee may see which ticket, how a multi-tenant classifier keeps client data separate, how sensitive pages stay out of a generated answer. Candidates who bolt access control on after the interviewer raises it score worse than those who put the permission filter in the retrieval path from the first diagram.

The third pattern is process attrition rather than a verdict. The loop can move in two-day increments and then stop dead: reschedules, cancellations, and long post-onsite silence including a report of a full month without contact. Keep other processes alive, and read a quiet recruiter as a signal about their capacity rather than about your performance.

## Data Source

Based on 4 candidate-reported interview experiences, primarily from 2026 Q1 through 2026 Q2.

## FAQ

**What is it like to work as a Machine Learning Engineer there?**
Candidate accounts cover interviews rather than the job, so treat this as context. The prompts are a fair preview of the work: retrieval and ranking over the company's own knowledge surfaces — issue tracker data, wiki pages, connected drives — feeding assistant and search experiences, backed by an internal ML platform that standardizes workflow orchestration and governance for production models. Work is distributed-first with no office-attendance requirement, and panels spanning Australia, New York and the Bay Area suggest ML teams are spread the same way.

**What is the engineering culture like?**
Values-forward and explicit about it: a values round scored on its own and a management round about mentoring, ambiguity and recovery from failure sit alongside the technical rounds, and interviewers are described as conversational rather than adversarial. On the ML side the emphasis reads as product engineering rather than research — production concerns, evaluation and the safety of generated answers come up more than novelty. One candidate did relay interviewers mentioning a dip in culture alongside recent review-cycle changes, so it is not a uniformly rosy picture.

**How hard is it to get in?**
The bar is a full engineering bar plus ML depth: you clear the same medium-difficulty data-structures rounds as any engineer, then a design round expecting retrieval, ranking, evaluation and access control in one conversation. Reported outcomes on this track skew toward rejection or long silence rather than offers, and the compressed schedule means the whole loop can land inside a few weeks with little time to prepare between rounds.

**Which round is hardest?**
By outcome, the algorithmic coding round — it is where the documented rejection happened, and it fails people for unfinished extensions rather than for a wrong approach. By content, the ML system design round punishes shallow answers hardest, especially on permission-aware retrieval and on proving the system works after launch. The resume deep dive is the most underestimated: it goes down to individual decisions on a single project.
